segments.text: Right now, you live in a world shaped by machines.
They ride code, diagnose diseases, and drive cars.
It feels like an unstoppable force
that appeared out of nowhere.
But the real answer is far stranger.
Why did this world-altering technology start
as a casual summer project?
The year was 1956.
Ten young scientists gathered on a quiet campus
in New Hampshire.
They did not have supercomputers,
internet databases, or massive funding.
They had only a bold, almost ridiculous belief.
Do you want to see how their overconfidence
shaped your modern life?
Dr. John McCarthy was a young mathematics professor.
He worked at Dartmouth College.
He wanted to bring together the brightest minds in computing,
mathematics, and psychology.
He wrote a proposal asking for a small grant.
What name did he choose to capture their wild ambition?
He wrote two words on the grant application.
Those words were artificial intelligence.
It was a clever marketing trick to distinguish their work
from cybernetics.
Many of his colleagues hated the term.
Why did his simple marketing phrase
capture the imagination of the world?
Dr. Marvin Minsky stood beside him.
He was a young researcher obsessed with neural networks.
They were joined by Dr. Claude Shannon,
the legendary founder of Information Theory.
They believed they could solve the mind in just two months.
Why were these giants of science so incredibly naive?
They had just witnessed the rapid rise of digital computers.
In less than a decade, machines had gone from basic calculators
to complex systems.
The scientists made a critical mistake.
Did they assume that logical reasoning
was the hardest part of intelligence?
Human vision is effortless for us.
Walking is a simple task.
We spent millions of years evolving to see,
balance, and move,
but only a few thousand years learning formal logic.
Computers could solve math,
but they could not recognize a cat.
Is it possible that we completely misunderstood
what makes us smart?
Two researchers arrived from Pittsburgh.
Their names were Dr. Allen Nuel and Dr. Herbert Simon.
They brought a program called the logic theorist
that proved 38 complex mathematical theorems.
Simon told his students they had built a thinking machine.
Why did this single success fuel such dangerous optimism?
Funding flowed into the universities.
Researchers made wild predictions.
They claimed that fully conscious machines
would exist within a single generation,
but by the late 1960s, the cracks began to show.
What happens when huge promises fail to deliver results?
The machines could play simple games.
They could not translate languages.
Translation software famously turned the spirit
is willing into the vodka is good.
The software lacked real-world experience.
Why did early AI systems struggle so much
with basic human communication?
The government cut off the funding.
The scientists returned to their homes.
Their overconfidence led to a sudden crash
known as the artificial intelligence winter.
Yet, the core idea is developed
during that summer never truly died.
How did a failed summer project
lay the foundation for the modern world?
We face the same challenges today.
The technology is much faster,
but we are still trying to teach machines
how to form abstract concepts.
The neural networks on your phone
are descendants of their math.
Are we still making the same mistakes
they made 70 years ago?
Tonight, you will interact with the machine.
You will not just use a tool.
You will participate in a casual summer project
that never ended.
